says: The policy details dialog names the policy section as "User or computer" when it applies to both, "Computer" for the machine side only, and "User" for the user side only.

The Supported-on button of the policy details dialog works only when the policy has a resolved support rule. Its text shows that rule's name; if the rule is missing but the policy names one, the text reads "<missing: " followed by the named rule and ">"; with none named it is blank.

The Category button works only when the policy has a resolved category. Its text shows the category name; if the category is missing but the policy names one, it reads "<orphaned from " followed by the category and ">"; a policy naming none reads "<uncategorized>".
The product details dialog labels a product "Major revision", "Minor revision" or "Top-level product" by its type, and shows a version only for revisions; a top-level product shows a blank version.
The product details dialog enables the Parent button and shows the parent name only when the product has a parent; otherwise both are blank or disabled.
The product details dialog lists the product's child revisions, each with its version and name; a product without children shows an empty list.
Double-clicking with no child selected in the product list does nothing; otherwise the dialog switches to show the chosen child product.
Clicking Parent in the product details dialog switches the dialog to show the parent product.
The support rule details dialog describes its logic as "Match all the referenced products", "Match any of the referenced products" or "Do not match products" according to the rule's logic type.
Each entry of a support rule shows the name of the support rule it references; if none, the name of the product; if neither exists, "<missing: " followed by the referenced product id and ">".
For a product entry that is a version range, the dialog shows its minimum and maximum versions, leaving a bound blank when the range has none. Entries that are not ranges show no versions.

Double-clicking with no entry selected does nothing. On a product entry the product details dialog opens; on a nested support rule entry this dialog switches to that rule; a missing reference does nothing.
Each time the download dialog opens, the destination defaults to the Windows PolicyDefinitions folder, the "open after download" folder is cleared and the dialog is idle.
Choosing a folder with Browse replaces the destination only when the person confirms the folder picker; cancelling leaves it unchanged.

When the Windows Installer extraction of the downloaded package exits with any non-zero code, the download fails at the step "extract the package"; the downloaded installer file is deleted only after a successful extraction.

Only when the person is a Windows administrator and the destination folder already exists, the download first takes ownership of the destination, giving the Administrators group ownership and full control, and enables the take-ownership and restore privileges.
Moving files into a destination replaces: any existing file with the same name is deleted first, then the new file is moved in. Missing destination folders are created.

When the person is an administrator, a newly created language folder and every moved file are reset to inherit permissions from their parent; a newly created main destination folder is not reset, and an existing folder gets ownership taken.

The download copies the main definition files, then the folder for the person's display language if the package has one, and also the English (en-US) language folder as a fallback whenever the language is not en-US.

If any step fails, the download stops, the dialog becomes idle again and the person is told "Failed to " followed by the step that failed ("create a scratch space", "download the package", "extract the package", "take control of the destination", "move the ADMX files" or "remove temporary files"), ending with a period.

When the download succeeds, the person is asked "ADMX files downloaded successfully. Open them now?"; only Yes makes the destination the new policy source folder to load. Either answer closes the dialog as accepted.

The raw policy file editor hides any value with an empty name. Keys are listed alphabetically, ignoring case, with sub-keys before the key's own values, nested by depth, and values are listed alphabetically, ignoring case.

The editor shows special value names as deletion markers: "**deletevalues" as "Delete values" with its data as text, a name starting "**del." as "Delete value" naming the value after it, and a name starting "**delvals" as "Delete all values". These entries are not editable values.
Other values are shown with their data as text: multi-strings joined by spaces, text and expandable text as-is, whole numbers as digits, and binary data as space-separated hex bytes.
After the list is rebuilt, the previous scroll position is restored if the list still has at least that many rows.

When adding a key, a blank name cancels silently. A name with a backslash is refused with "The key name is not valid.", and a name already used beside it with "The key name is already taken.". Otherwise the key is created under the selected key, or at the top if none is selected, and selected.
A new key is stored in the policy file as an empty entry with no value kind.

Value data is requested in a dialog suited to the kind: text for string and expandable string, a number for 32-bit and 64-bit numbers, lines for multi-string. Any other kind is refused with "This value kind is not supported." and nothing changes.

When adding a value, its starting data is empty text for string kinds, 0 for numeric kinds and an empty list for multi-string; the value is saved to the selected key only if the person confirms both dialogs.

Deleting a key offers three choices. Purge removes everything in the key; clear-first marks the key cleared before re-adding its direct, non-deletion values; otherwise a deletion entry is written for the value name the person typed.
Re-adding after "clear first" restores only the key's values shown one level directly below it, skipping deletion markers and values of sub-keys.
Deleting a single value in the list writes a deletion entry for it, and the list then shows it as "Delete value"; it does not simply drop the value (that is Forget).

Using Forget on a key asks "Are you sure you want to remove this key and all its contents?"; on No nothing changes. On Yes the key, all its sub-keys, their values and clearances are removed from the file.
Forgetting a value removes it from the file with no confirmation, and selection returns to its key.
Editing a value keeps its name and kind and replaces its data with what the person confirms, ignoring the change if cancelled.
Pressing Save accepts the changes made to the policy file.
Pressing Escape cancels the dialog.
While an ADMX download is running, the download dialog cannot be closed.

While a download is running, the Close, Start, destination box and Browse controls are disabled, and the progress text and a moving spinner are shown; when idle they are enabled and the spinner is still.
The download fetches one fixed Microsoft package, Administrative Templates for Windows 11 Sep 2026 Update (26H2), and takes definitions from its fixed folder inside the unpacked package.

statement: The download assumes Microsoft still serves the fixed Windows 11 26H2 package at its link, with definitions at the expected folder inside it. If not, the download fails with a step message.

assumed.why: The package link and its internal folder layout are on Microsoft's server, outside the code.
assumed.ifWrong: Downloads fail at the download or move step, and the person cannot fetch definitions from within the program.

evidence.shows: The package link and the folder inside it are fixed constants.

says: Deleting a key opens a dialog with three choices; nothing is confirmed until one is selected, and Escape cancels. Purge empties the key: all its values are destroyed and the key is marked cleared. Clear-first does the same, but first drops the key's old cleared mark so the new one sorts ahead of the values, then puts back the key's own values listed one level directly below it, skipping deletion markers and sub-key values. Delete-one writes a deletion entry for a typed value name and keeps the key's other contents; it is confirmed only when a name is typed, otherwise the person is told "You must enter a value name." and the dialog stays open. After any choice the list is rebuilt and the key is selected.

The download copies the main definition files, then the language folder named after the person's regional-format setting in Windows (not the display language) if the package has one; a missing own-language folder is skipped. When that setting is not en-US it also copies the en-US folder as a fallback, and here the folder is required: if the package lacks it, the download fails at "move the ADMX files".

Using Forget on a key asks "Are you sure you want to remove this key and all its contents?"; on No nothing changes. On Yes the key, all its sub-keys, their values and clearances are removed from the file, the list is rebuilt and the key's parent is selected (its ancestors are selected in turn). A top-level key has no parent, so nothing is selected and the buttons are refreshed to match.

Value data is requested in a dialog suited to the kind: text for string and expandable string, a number for 32-bit and 64-bit numbers, lines for multi-string. Any other kind is refused with "This value kind is not supported.". When the person cancels a dialog, or the kind is refused, no data is returned and callers change nothing.

If any step fails, the download stops, the dialog becomes idle again and the person is told "Failed to " followed by the step that failed ("create a scratch space", "download the package", "extract the package", "take control of the destination", "move the ADMX files" or "remove temporary files"), ending with a period. Nothing is rolled back: files already moved into the destination stay, and the scratch folder is deleted only as the last step, so an earlier failure leaves it behind. A failure at "remove temporary files" comes after the files were installed.

The destination text is not checked before the download starts: empty or invalid text is passed on and the download fails at "move the ADMX files". A person who is not a Windows administrator skips the ownership step and proceeds, so a protected destination fails at the move.
